speedupBasis: All 4 nodes run inside one Java process on one machine, so they share its 16 available processors (as reported by the JVM; inside a container this can be lower than the machine's). The speedup cannot exceed 4, the smaller of the node count and that processor count, and other work on the machine lowers it further. For small matrices the scatter of A, the broadcast of B and the gather of C take longer than the multiply they split up, so the parallel run can be slower than the sequential one (a speedup below 1). Each node's compute time is measured on the node, around its multiply only; every other time is measured on the root. 1 untimed warm-up product was run first, so the JIT had compiled the multiply before the timed runs. The timed sequential product runs after 1 warm-up product and the timed parallel run after 2 full products (the warm-up and the sequential product), so the parallel run meets a slightly warmer JIT and processor cache than the sequential product did. Nothing else on the cluster is paused during a run: Experiment 1 calls, MPI collectives, Experiment 2 requests and other experiments can use the same nodes and processors at the same time, and any such work is included in these figures.
algorithmNote: The root splits A into blocks of whole rows, one block per live node in rank order, and scatters them; it broadcasts the whole of B; every node multiplies its rows by B at the same time on its own Experiment 2 executor; then the root fetches the blocks of C one by one in rank order, assembles C and compares it bit for bit with the sequential product. The scatter and the broadcast are Experiment 9's linear collectives over Experiment 1's RMI (link L6). A failed transfer or compute leaves a hole that is reported, never filled in.
phaseTimeLabel: The scatter and broadcast times are Experiment 9's total collective times, measured on the root from just before the first remote transfer to just after the last. They include the root's own work between transfers (serializing each request again to size it, and computing checksums), so they are longer than the time on the wire.
payloadGenerationNote: Generating A and B is timed once on the root, before the timed parts, for information only. The scatter and the broadcast generate A and B again from the seed inside the parallel run; that time falls into the other time and nothing is subtracted for it.
fairnessNote: The timed sequential product runs after 1 warm-up product and the timed parallel run after 2 full products (the warm-up and the sequential product), so the parallel run meets a slightly warmer JIT and processor cache than the sequential product did.
otherActivityNote: Nothing else on the cluster is paused during a run: Experiment 1 calls, MPI collectives, Experiment 2 requests and other experiments can use the same nodes and processors at the same time, and any such work is included in these figures.
experimentTwoSideEffect: Each node multiplies its rows on its own Experiment 2 executor, which runs only while that node's request listener is running. Starting this experiment, or running it, therefore starts the request listener of every live node that does not have one yet, on its requests port (7201 to 7205 here). The matrix never stops these listeners and a cluster reset does not either; a listener closes only when its node crashes or the backend stops. The matrix work shows in Experiment 2's live executor statistics, but not in its request history or its events, and Experiment 2's status stays idle meanwhile.
firstRunNote: Before every run, outside the timed parts, the module makes sure that each live node's request listener is running, so no listener start is timed. The first run after a start or a reset still pays first-use costs that cannot be moved out of the run: loading RMI stub classes, opening the first connections to each node, starting the first worker thread of each node's executor, and the first use of the collective and checksum code; these fall into the scatter, broadcast, compute-phase and gather times, never into a node's own compute time. The multiply itself is warmed up by the warm-up products. Run a size again to see it without these costs; the series uses the newest complete run of each size.
collectiveIdsNote: A run's scatter of A and broadcast of B use collective ids 1000000000 + 2 x run id and that + 1, so they never meet Experiment 9's own ids, which count from 1. The nodes keep them like any collective, so they also appear among each node's kept ids on the MPI page.
collectiveLatencyBasis: Measured on the root around the whole transfer: a fresh lookup of CollectiveEndpoint in the target node's RMI registry (including RMI's distributed garbage collection "dirty" call when this process holds no other live stub for that endpoint), then the method call with its arguments and reply over a real loopback socket. Experiment 1 shows the lookup and the call as separate figures; here they are one.
computeRoundTripBasis: Measured on the root around one remote compute call: a fresh lookup of MatrixEndpoint in the node's RMI registry (including RMI's distributed garbage collection "dirty" call when this process holds no other live stub for it), the call, the node's queue wait and multiply on its Experiment 2 executor, and the reply. The node's compute time, around the multiply only, is measured on the node.
gatherLatencyBasis: Measured on the root around one fetch of a block of C: a fresh lookup of MatrixEndpoint in the node's RMI registry (including RMI's distributed garbage collection "dirty" call when this process holds no other live stub for it), then the call and its reply over a real loopback socket.
payloadSizeBasis: Java serialization size (java.io ObjectOutputStream, stream header included); not the RMI wire bytes; primitive parameters are sized as primitives, as RMI marshals them
seriesRule: For each configured series size, the newest kept run of that size that completed and matched the sequential product. A size without such a run is listed as not run, never as 0. Runs of other sizes are only in the history.

glossary.label: Sequential time
glossary.definition: Around the multiply of the whole matrix only, on the root, after the warm-up products and before the parallel run.

glossary.label: Generating A and B
glossary.definition: Around generating A and B once, before the timed parts. Informational: the collectives generate them again inside the parallel run, and nothing is subtracted for it.

glossary.label: Scatter of A
glossary.definition: Experiment 9's total time of the scatter, from just before the first remote transfer to just after the last; it includes the root's sizing and checksum work between transfers.

glossary.label: Broadcast of B
glossary.definition: Experiment 9's total time of the broadcast, from just before the first remote transfer to just after the last; it includes the root's sizing and checksum work between transfers.

glossary.label: Compute phase
glossary.definition: From just before the first compute is dispatched to when the last compute (a node's reply or the root's own block) is known: the computation time of the parallel run.

glossary.label: Gather of C
glossary.definition: From just before the first fetch to just after the last; unknown when no fetch was made.

glossary.label: Parallel time
glossary.definition: From just before the scatter to the end of the last phase that ran; one interval, not a sum.

glossary.label: Compute round trip
glossary.definition: Measured on the root around one remote compute call: a fresh lookup of MatrixEndpoint in the node's RMI registry (including RMI's distributed garbage collection "dirty" call when this process holds no other live stub for it), the call, the node's queue wait and multiply on its Experiment 2 executor, and the reply. The node's compute time, around the multiply only, is measured on the node.

glossary.label: Fetch latency
glossary.definition: Measured on the root around one fetch of a block of C: a fresh lookup of MatrixEndpoint in the node's RMI registry (including RMI's distributed garbage collection "dirty" call when this process holds no other live stub for it), then the call and its reply over a real loopback socket.

glossary.label: Time to failure
glossary.definition: From just before a call until its failure was known; not a latency.

glossary.label: Node compute time
glossary.definition: Around that rank's multiply only, on the node; queue wait excluded.

glossary.label: Communication time
glossary.definition: Scatter + broadcast + gather; unknown if any of them is unknown.

glossary.label: Other time
glossary.definition: Parallel time - communication time - compute phase: the root's own work between the phases. It can be negative because the parts are measured separately, and it is never clamped.

glossary.label: Speedup
glossary.definition: Sequential time / parallel time: the measured speedup, only for a complete run whose result matched the sequential product.

glossary.label: Compute-bound speedup
glossary.definition: Sequential time / the slowest node compute time: what the multiply alone would allow if communication cost nothing; never the measured speedup.

coHosting.reason: All nodes run inside one backend process on one computer, so they share its processors and memory: they are separate nodes sharing a machine, not separate machines. Every scatter, broadcast, compute call and fetch still goes through the target node's own RMI registry and a stub over a real loopback socket, so those times are real and measured; only the network distance between the nodes is missing.
